<reason>Side B won a closely fought, high-quality clash. B's throughline — "origin is the trigger" — survived every exchange: natives who fail every civic and linguistic benchmark keep full membership, so an adoption requirement attached only to immigrants is probation, not reciprocity. A's best counters (different starting points, the driver's test, compulsory schooling as the "same bar") were each blunted: B distinguished licenses from membership and noted immigrant children already sit in the compulsory classrooms, so the only remaining demand is adult absorption no native ever faces. B also answered A's pressure questions more honestly than A acknowledged — proactive enforcement tools (inspectors, hotlines, truancy rules) directly addressed the "no complaint arrives" scenario, yet A's closing falsely called that answer empty. Conversely, B caught a real internal tension in A's case: A located the value of norms "where no policeman can go," then defined adoption by observable conduct — "a funded class can teach words; it cannot conscript a kitchen." A's A4.2 move (claiming B's demand for an observable test conceded adoption has observable content) was clever but sophistic. A still landed real points on empowerment via language and the civic/cultural distinction, and crystallized well, but slightly overclaimed a knockout from a concession B had already contextualized. B's execution — direct A1/A2 answers, consistent thread, and memorable reframes ("second constitution," "performance review") — made the debate easier to decide for CON.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side B's Rebuttal 2 (B4.5–B4.6): after A defined adoption by observable conduct like school enrollment and language classes, B exposed that A's own case located the real stakes inside families beyond any test — "a funded class can teach words; it cannot conscript a kitchen" — puncturing A's observable-standard answer and cementing the asymmetry argument that native adults skip the same inner joining daily and keep the franchise.</best_rebuttal>
